findings: PARTIALLY_ANSWERABLE: C is the only modalised option ('may have been written down'); A, B and D are flat assertions carrying hard numbers. A stem asking what we are TOLD about a record book pairs naturally with a stated caveat about that record's reliability, and the modal marks C as that caveat.

PARTIALLY_ANSWERABLE: D's arithmetic ('three of the four people who have kept it wrote up the first nine springs') and A's tidy coincidence (the counts begin the very year the mill stopped) are both constructed-distractor shapes.
justification: I could not verify any of the four claims - none is checkable without the passage or the counts themselves. The only usable signal is modality: exactly one option is hedged, and the stem asks what we are told about the record rather than what the record shows, which favours a stated reliability caveat. That gets me to roughly 40 percent on C, above the 25 percent base but nowhere near decisive. I could not tell whether the 1931 mill date, the netting comparison or the four keepers are true, nor which species the book actually covers.

findings: CROSS_QUESTION: q3's stem presupposes as established fact that 'so few dace get above the weir', and q5's options C and D both frame the whole text as a pass that mostly does not work. In that frame D - most grayling that entered did not reach the top pool - is the option the rest of the page has already made likely.
PARTIALLY_ANSWERABLE: B states a generic truth about pool-and-weir passes rather than anything specific to grayling, and reads as filler for a stem asking what the study found about grayling.
justification: Blind I cannot check the temperature result (A), the resting claim (B) or the size-versus-build attribution (C). The lift comes entirely off the surrounding page: q3's stem asserts dace failure as given and q5 offers two summary options built on failure, so a failure statistic here is thematically pre-endorsed. About 50 percent on D. I could not tell whether the study measured temperature at all, and C's size/build distinction would need fisheries knowledge I would not expect a student to have.

findings: PARTIALLY_ANSWERABLE: A is the longest option and the only one with a two-clause causal structure ('they come up the bank opposite the entrance, AND too little flows from it to draw them over'); B, C and D are single-clause reasons.

CROSS_QUESTION: q5-D asserts 'the different reason in each case' and q2-D places grayling failure INSIDE the pass. Under a different-reason-per-species reading, B - the fall between pools being too much for a small fish - duplicates that in-pass mechanism and is disfavoured, narrowing this question to A, C and D.
justification: All four reasons are real documented causes of coarse-fish failure at passes - attraction flow (A), excessive inter-pool drop (B), seasonal mismatch (C) and shoaling behaviour (D) - so domain knowledge does not single one out. What tips me is form, A being markedly the most textured, plus the cross-question narrowing above. About 45 percent on A. I could not determine when the pass opens, what the drop between pools is, or whether dace shoaling is discussed at all.

findings: PARTIALLY_ANSWERABLE: the stem asks what is IMPLIED and A is the only modalised option ('probably heavier than the river usually brings'). An inference-shaped stem paired with the single inference-shaped option is a form match.

PARTIALLY_ANSWERABLE (unit-level tic): this is the second item in the unit where exactly one option carries a hedge and the hedged option is the one form selects (see q1). A generator that reliably hedges the key is a systematic channel even where each instance is individually weak.
justification: A, C and D share the presupposition that one orifice blocked and one stayed clear, with B alone on a different axis (why they were cut). Per the batch20 calibration rule I do not score that 3+1 - the cluster holds the key at 0.75 and each member at 0.25, exactly base rate. The only genuine lift is the modality match with 'implied', putting A at about 40 percent. I could not tell which orifice blocked, whether the February spate was exceptional, or what the orifices were cut for.

findings: CROSS_QUESTION: the four sibling stems (a counts book at the trap, grayling in the pass, why so few dace get above the weir, two orifices cut in 2023) eliminate A and B outright - no stem touches consequences for the river above (A) or an argument about how a pass should be judged (B). That leaves a two-way choice holding roughly 0.90 of the mass, a far heavier concentration than the 2+2 pair the calibration rule already counts as a channel.

CROSS_QUESTION: within the surviving pair, D's 'two others mostly do not' maps onto exactly the two species the sibling stems name (grayling in q2, dace in q3), and q1-C's mention of chub supplies the third species D requires.
justification: This is the strongest residual channel in the batch and it is entirely student-available: all five stems sit on one page, so a student who reads them knows the text covers a counts book, grayling, dace and a 2023 modification, which kills A and B without any passage. Between C and D I genuinely cannot decide - D matches the question set's species structure, but D also asserts a species that ascends easily, which no stem corroborates, and that unsupported extra is itself a distractor shape. I put D at about 48 percent and C at about 42 percent, so no single option reaches the 60 percent kill bar, but the two-of-four elimination is severe.

A cloze gap with the passage withheld gives literally no context - the option list is the entire evidence. earned / gained / returned / fetched are all idiomatic with a sum of money, so nothing is excluded on collocation. I took 'fetched' only because it is the most marked and precise of the four and generators often build near-synonym distractors around a precise key, but that heuristic is equally consistent with 'fetched' being the trap. About 30 percent, inside the chance band.

Four inflected forms of one lemma (keep / kept / keeping / to keep). Which form fits is fixed entirely by the syntax of the withheld sentence, so this gap is informationally inert stems-only: no length, register or semantic asymmetry exists to exploit. I picked 'to keep' arbitrarily. 25 to 28 percent, chance.

clearance / giveaway / markdown / liquidation are four retail-disposal nouns. The one thing form offers is register: 'giveaway' is markedly informal and would sit oddly in the formal register the rest of this batch suggests, which nudges it down. But that eliminates at most one option and leaves my top pick, 'clearance' (the commonest collocate of 'sale'), at about 33 percent - not enough to name a channel. I could not tell whether the gap is a modifier, a head noun, or part of a fixed phrase.

amply / briefly / thinly / openly do not share a semantic field - they span quantity, duration and manner. 'amply' and 'thinly' are near-antonyms on the quantity axis, so if the gap is about quantity they hold 0.5 between them; but 0.5 is the base rate for any two options and yields no gain on either, and I cannot tell from the list alone whether the gap concerns quantity at all. My pick of 'amply' is close to a three-way toss. About 28 percent.

Still / Granted / Therefore / Afterwards span concession (two of them), consequence and time. 'Afterwards' is the weakest fit for a sentence-initial connective in argumentative prose, a mild elimination, but the other three stay live and the two concessives do not discriminate against each other. 'Still' is the commoner concessive so I took it, at about 30 percent. Without the sentences either side of the gap there is nothing else to use. The whole cloze is well insulated stems-only, which is expected - no passage means no gap context at all.

findings: WORLD_KNOWLEDGE: paper-conservation knowledge makes D near-certainly false - solvent removal of pressure-sensitive tape adhesive is well known NOT to lift the brown staining out of the fibres - and makes C's account (adhesive penetrating the sheet and leaving it translucent) the standard description of a degraded clear-tape mend. This route needs domain knowledge a Swedish 18-year-old will not have.

PARTIALLY_ANSWERABLE: D's additive 'as well' is an over-reach shape - the option claims the treatment does the hard second job for free - and B's chiastic symmetry (heat for hardened adhesive, solvent for still-soft) is the tidy-rule shape distractors take. A test-wise student can shave both on form alone and land near C at roughly 35 to 40 percent.
justification: As an expert reader I get to about 50 percent on C via conservation knowledge, well above chance but under the kill bar; a Swedish 18-year-old with only form to go on reaches roughly 35 to 40 percent by the same two eliminations. Neither route is decisive, because the stem asks what Fenniscarth says and a passage is free to make a point other than the textbook one. I could not check A's plasticiser-oxidation mechanism or its timing claim, and I could not tell whether the text distinguishes carrier from adhesive at all.

The stem's 'concluded' mildly disfavours B and C, which are stated-rule and stated-governance shapes rather than inferences, leaving A and D as the ledger-derived conclusions. But A, B and D already form a 3+1 against C on the records axis, and per the calibration rule that cluster is inert. The residual cue is generic to the question type rather than specific to this option set, and my top pick, A, sits at about 33 percent. Option lengths are evenly matched at 14 to 15 words each, so there is no length cue. I could not tell whether a fine schedule, a reservation queue or an annual purchasing meeting existed.

Historically both A (moving out when the hay ran out) and C (the byastämmans decision plus how far lövsprickningen had come) are real determinants of the buföring date, so domain knowledge does not separate them, and B and D are also defensible. C is the longest option and the only one naming an institution, and compound two-criterion options are a mild key shape, but that reaches only about 32 percent. q4-D's mention of winter fodder and outland grazing gives A a weak cross-question nudge the other way, flattening the field further. Chance-adjacent; nothing nameable reaches a single option.

findings: WORLD_KNOWLEDGE: the standard account of kulning is that each vallkullas call was her own and recognised by her own animals, while horn signals were conventionalised messages. D states exactly that contrast. This is Swedish cultural knowledge some 18-year-olds will have, so the channel is partly student-available.

PARTIALLY_ANSWERABLE: D is the only option drawing a conceptual contrast (idiosyncratic versus fixed meaning); A, B and C all contrast circumstances (weather, time of day, purpose). Being the odd one out on the KIND of distinction is the interesting-claim shape a text builds a question on.
justification: About 50 percent on D, the highest single-option credence in the LÄS units. I could not verify anything about carrying distance in wind (A), a dawn/evening split (B) or predator-scaring (C) - all three are plausible and C in particular is a real folk belief. The lift is a cultural prior plus D being the only option whose contrast is about meaning rather than circumstance. Below the kill bar but a genuine channel.

findings: WORLD_KNOWLEDGE: Swedish farm servants were engaged by the tjänsteår rather than by the season, so D is the historically correct structural fact. Reaching it needs history a Swedish 18-year-old may only half have.

PARTIALLY_ANSWERABLE: D is the only option that refuses the stem's premise - the other three answer 'how was the summer's pay arranged' while D says the pay was not organised by summer at all. Premise-refusing options are a recognisable key shape.
justification: About 42 percent on D. A (agreed in spring, largely paid in kind) is also historically true, which is what keeps this off the kill line, and B's production-linked pay and C's pay-on-sale are both defensible enough that I cannot exclude them. B carries the only hedge in the set ('varierade något'), a competing form cue pointing the other way which I discounted because the premise-refusal shape is the stronger of the two. I could not tell what the text actually says about the form or the timing of payment.

findings: CROSS_QUESTION: the three sibling stems ask about the timing of the buföring, the difference between the calls and the horn signals, and how the fäbod people were paid. All three are about the people and their summer work, which is A. No stem touches a dairy or the end of the fäbod system, so C is eliminated from the page alone.

PARTIALLY_ANSWERABLE: with C gone the field is three, and A is the only heading whose two halves are both covered by sibling stems; B and D each draw only on a single option elsewhere in the unit (q3-B's butter and cheese, q1-A's hay).
justification: About 45 percent on A. The counter-cue is real and is why this is not higher: HP heading keys are often the analytic option rather than the one that just names the surface subject, and B and D are the analytic-shaped pair here, so a student trained on that heuristic might go the other way. What I could not do is tell whether the text closes on the decline of the system, the one thing that would rescue C, or whether preservation and transport (B) form a real strand rather than an incidental detail.

findings: CROSS_QUESTION: q2's option set reveals that the unit is a debate about moving the market off the square onto a field, with three of its four options endorsing a move. The standard premise of such an argument is that the square has run out of room, which is precisely q1-D - sixteen applicants left without a place. The option supplying the argument's premise is the one the neighbouring question has already made likely.
WORLD_KNOWLEDGE: q1-C ('new applicants usually go before the old ones') inverts ordinary market-stall practice, where incumbents hold their pitches, and reads as a constructed false statement.
justification: About 42 percent on D. B and D are table facts I cannot check without the passage, and A (allotment by lot) is a real practice somewhere, so nothing is excluded on knowledge alone. The lift is the cross-question premise supply plus C's implausibility. I could not verify the number sixteen, could not check how often place 1 changed hands, and could not tell whether the text describes a queue, a lottery or an inherited pitch.

A, B and D all say move to the field and C alone says stay: a three-way cluster against a single outsider, which the batch20 calibration rule makes informationally inert - the cluster holds the key at 0.75 and each member at 0.25, exactly base rate. Nothing separates A, B and D. D is the hedged compromise (a one-year trial), which cuts both ways, since debate pieces key on firm stands as often as on measured ones, and A's and B's added conditions are equally specific. I picked A essentially at random among the three, about 30 percent. I could not tell what the writer's actual objection to the square is.

findings: WORLD_KNOWLEDGE: the Swedish finrum was kept for honoured guests and formal occasions while everyday callers were received in the kitchen. That is D, and it makes B its explicit negation. Partly student-available - the convention is still culturally recognisable, though weakening with each cohort.

PAIR_STRUCTURE: B and D are contradictories on one variable (is the closed room for the closest or for the most honoured). The cultural prior breaks that pair almost entirely toward D rather than leaving it split at 0.25 each.
PARTIALLY_ANSWERABLE (stem-internal): the stem's own descriptor 'det stängda rummet' tells a passage-blind reader that the room was normally shut, which argues against B before any option is read.
justification: About 42 percent on D. What holds it down is that A is genuinely live - strangers on business being shown into the fine room while kin went straight to the kitchen is a real ethnographic pattern and a more interesting point for a text to make, which is exactly the kind of claim a LÄS item gets built on. C is a weaker version of the same formality idea. So the world knowledge points at D but the item may be constructed to defeat that prior. See the pair line for the q2 leak that compounds this.

A and C share the presupposition that the set eventually left the room, so that proposition does leak from the option set, but it is non-discriminating: it does not separate A from C and is compatible with B and D. Beyond it two cues pull opposite ways. 'Vad kan man dra för slutsats' is the shape that usually keys a computed fact, favouring D's more-than-ten-years; C is the option pitched at the altitude of the whole text (where the household's evenings happened) and reuses the kitchen/closed-room contrast the unit is built on, favouring C. I have them at roughly 33 and 32 percent, so the pair holds about two thirds between them but neither is picked out. I could not tell when the set arrived, when or whether it moved, or whether the room was refurnished.

findings: ONE-WAY LEAK (q2 into q1, STRONG form): the proposition 'the square is unsatisfactory and a move to the field is seriously on the table' is asserted by three of q2's four options (A, B and D), so it survives non-resolution - a passage-blind reader acquires it whichever option is the key. It bears directly on q1's variable, because the standard premise of a move-the-market argument is that the square has run out of pitches, which is q1-D. Lift on q1-D from 0.25 to roughly 0.40.

ONE-WAY LEAK (weak, single-option): q2-C's clause 'Torghandlarnas flertal har rätt' presupposes that the sitting traders are an organised constituency with a majority view, consistent with an incumbency system, which mildly disfavours q1-A (lottery) and q1-C (new before old). This proposition sits in only one option and therefore does NOT survive non-resolution.

SYMMETRIC VOUCHING (partial): both sets are drawn from one small factual world - this square, these applicants, this field, this market - and corroborate each other on a single shared variable, scarcity of pitches. q1-C and q1-D imply scarcity, which supports q2's move cluster; q2's move cluster implies scarcity, which supports q1-D. The vouching runs through that one variable rather than across the whole factual world.
justification: JOINT stems-only solvability: the unit is NOT jointly solvable. q2 is inert on its own - three options endorse moving and one opposes, a 3+1 the calibration rule bars me from scoring, and nothing separates the three movers - so the leak has no resolved source. But its strong form does not need one, because the surviving proposition sits in three of the four options, and that alone moves q1. Reverse direction: q1's options say nothing about the writer's stance beyond a weak scarcity hint carried by two rival options (C and D), which does not survive non-resolution, so the leak is effectively one-way, q2 into q1. Answering q2 does shift q1 - q2 in {A,B,D} hardens the scarcity premise and lifts q1-D, while q2 = C would undercut it - whereas answering q1 barely moves q2 at all. Net: one real one-way channel worth roughly 15 points on q1-D, and no joint solvability.

findings: ONE-WAY LEAK (q2 into q1, STRONG form): the proposition 'the closed room was not the household's ordinary everyday social space' is carried independently by two of q2's options - A's 'Rummet stod orört sedan apparaten burits ut' and C's 'Kvällarna hamnade i köket, dit apparaten till slut flyttades' - and so survives non-resolution. It bears directly on q1's variable and removes q1-B (those one socialised with most) almost entirely, lifting the remaining three from 0.25 to about 0.33 before any cultural prior is applied.

ONE-WAY LEAK (clause level): q2-C's second clause names the kitchen as where the evenings ended up, which is the exact fine-room-versus-kitchen division q1 tests. A passage-blind reader who reads q2 first has been handed the unit's central spatial contrast before answering q1.

SYMMETRIC VOUCHING (moderate but lopsided): one house, two rooms, one television and a set of callers is a very small factual world, so members of each set corroborate members of the other on the shared variable 'how special and how closed was the room'. The corroboration is asymmetric - q2's clauses say a great deal about q1's variable, while no q1 option mentions the set, the kitchen or any date.

PARTIALLY_ANSWERABLE (compounding, stem-internal): q1's own stem says 'det stängda rummet', pre-answering part of the question, since a normally shut room is not where you receive the people you see most. It stacks with the q2 leak on the same option.
justification: JOINT stems-only solvability: the unit is PARTIALLY solvable, and the solvable half is q1. Combining the stem word 'stängda', the shared presupposition in q2-A and q2-C, and ordinary Swedish knowledge of the finrum, a blind reader can discard q1-B outright and reach roughly 0.42 on q1-D. q2 itself stays near chance: A and C share the departure presupposition without separating from each other, and the competing 'slutsats implies a computed fact' cue points at D instead. Information therefore flows one way - answering q2 shifts q1, since picking A or C hardens the special-room reading and pushes q1 further from B and toward D or A, while answering q1 does not shift q2 at all because no q1 option touches the television, the kitchen or any date. This is the stronger of the two pair leaks in the batch, the surviving proposition being more specific and landing on the very variable q1 tests, but it still carries no single q1 option past the kill bar.
